I had the opportunity to break ground once years ago, when I was a young man of 20 years or so. It was a side lot between two properties that technically we owned but was buried under several mounds of fully mature pampas and bordered on one side by a steep hill and fence. Inside a giant pampas mound attached to the hillside was a massive bumblebee nest. I didn't think they made nests but it sure seemed that way.

As much as I loved the bumblebees, I wanted that land and did some research. Sure enough, South American pampas grass is an invasive species, so I have few qualms about reclaiming my 9 square feet of heaven with a machete. The bees fought back fiercely but I counter attack'd with the garden hose. I expelled them slowly to give them time to forage a new home, and after a month they had surrendered the hillside clump altogether.

These heroic efforts took most of the summer, the highlight of which was the time I attempted to burn a pampas mound. I had 7 buckets of water prepared in advance, and within 5 minutes of setting it alight I had expended all but one in a fevered attempt to put out a rising inferno that soon threatened to singe the eaves of the nearby trees. Thereafter I resorted to manual labor solely, and focused on reducing alien foliage with the machete. By October I was an ace swordsman, or so I believed.

Then the wet season arrived, and after the first good rain I was able to dig out the root bases of the pampas, which are shallow and easily leveraged from underneath. This was the point where people wondered what I was doing over there.

Fall descended quickly that year, and time was spent with friends and family for several weeks at a time. In between days I gathered the slain pampas grass into a pile a meter tall and wide and pressed it with a plywood board and a discarded tire. As winter passed I turned the pile every three weeks or so, and as spring beckoned I spread the mulch over the virgin soil.

In April the rains continued intermittently, now lightly precipitating, now pouring in violent showers. During the breaks I truly began to break ground in my new garden. I discovered the topsoil was a mere 2 inches before hitting a layer of clay. Undeterred, I dug as much the clay as I could muster with the shovel, to an average depth of about a half meter, less in places due to extensive tree roots coming from the old trees on the hillside above the fence.

By the beginning of May I had amended the plot with a few bags of prime nursery soil and began planting in earnest. It was about this time the neighborhood cats began a low key turf war for the garden.

I quickly planted herbs and leafy greens, and they amazingly grew beyond my expectations. I had to put a wire cage over the catnip to keep it alive.

By July I was harvesting a salad a day from the yard just to keep up with growth and thanks were received from the recipients. It was time well spent.

I currently have 4 round (I'll explain why later) beds, each about 4 meters in diameter. They were created in what was a horse padock. Initially, there was only a couple of inches of soil covering white clay which was the consistency of wet cement in winter and dry cement in summer.

The beds are round because I use a hemispherical dome made of 3/4" PVC pipe and chicken wire as a movable chicken coop. Initially, or when a crop is done, the dome is placed over the bed and chickens added (I have 3 Australorps in there as they're pretty good diggers ). After a little while (usually several weeks) the chickens will have pretty much eaten everything green. They've also pooped everywhere too and laid eggs for me. The dome is then moved to the next bed.

For the first run I needed to dig the top 3-4 inches and manually remove remaining weed roots (mostly cooch grass and dock) that would regrow otherwise. Then i added as much home made compost, horse poop and sheep poop as i could get before planting. I also add a bit of crushed limestone to help break up the clay.

It's now been about 3 years since I started and the beds are beginning to get quite good. The soil is now as deep as my fork will go. I generally rotate through tomatoes & zuchini, corn and broad beans with silver beet, cabbage, dichon radish and wombok. Much of the silver beet gets feed to the chickens giving me really tasty eggs. The dichon and wombok is used to make Kimchi, have also made sauerkraut with the cabbage.

More recently, I've been experimenting with making my own biochar. I have a basically limitless supply of sticks to turn into charcoal when i can get them dry outside of the fire restrictions (a pretty small window).

More tomatoes and zuchini than I can eat right now, which isn't a bad problem to have.
